title: The Priests' Bank: Roberto Calvi from Via Clerici to Blackfriars Bridge
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Milan, the banker's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi agree on the date. General city coordinates: no source gives the birth address.
stops.campa: Milan is a banking city before it is anything else, and on the thirteenth of April 1920 a son is born in it to a manager of the Banca Commerciale Italiana. They name him Roberto. He grows up inside the vocabulary of the trade: current accounts, correspondents, the discipline of a ledger that has to balance before the doors close. His father's institution is one of the three great Italian banks and it will be Roberto's own first employer. The household is a bank manager's household, salaried and Catholic and exact about money, and the career it points the boy toward is his father's own.
suggested_refs: The Milan headquarters of the Banca Commerciale Italiana, the father's employer and the son's first

stops.name: Milan, enrolled at the Bocconi
stops.date_confidence: year attested (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi); no month or day given. The pin marks the institution, not the 1939 building: the Bocconi moved to the Via Sarfatti campus only in 1941 (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universita_commerciale_Luigi_Bocconi), so the coordinate is an anachronism for the year of enrollment and is used deliberately, with the older seat unlocated in any fetched source.
stops.campa: After the liceo classico he enrolls in the Faculty of Economics and Commerce at the Universita Bocconi, the private business school Milan built for its own merchant class. What follows the enrollment is the war, which takes the years the degree would have taken. He comes back from service to the counter of a bank rather than to a lecture hall, carrying what the Bocconi teaches the sons of the merchant class: accounting and foreign exchange, the mechanics by which money in one currency is made into money in another.
suggested_refs: The Universita commerciale Luigi Bocconi, Milan, and its pre-1941 seat

stops.name: Piazza della Scala, the father's bank
stops.date_confidence: the sources disagree and the disagreement is not resolved here. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi has him joining the Banca Commerciale Italiana after wartime service and only then moving to the Ambrosiano; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi dates only his 1947 entry to the Ambrosiano and describes no BCI period at all. The 1945 date is a placeholder for 'after the war' and rests on the English article alone. Coordinates are the bank's historic Milan headquarters; the branch is not identified.
stops.campa: He begins where his father worked, at the Banca Commerciale Italiana, whose Milanese headquarters stand on the Piazza della Scala across from the opera house. It is the orthodox opening move: a large, solid, state-linked institution, the kind of place where a careful man spends forty years and retires known to three hundred colleagues by his surname. Calvi spends two or three. The record of this passage is thin and the two encyclopedic accounts of it do not agree; what they agree on is the direction of travel, out of the great bank and into a smaller and stranger one a few streets north.
suggested_refs: The Banca Commerciale Italiana headquarters, Piazza della Scala, Milan

stops.name: Via Clerici, entering the Ambrosiano
stops.date_confidence: year attested on both language articles; no month or day. The pin is the atlas's canonical Banco Ambrosiano coordinate, inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json and michele_sindona.journey.json; an independent geocode of the bank's stated address, Via Clerici 2, gives 45.46674, 9.18743, about 115 m away. The 1952 marriage is attested by year only.
stops.campa: The Banco Ambrosiano was founded in 1896 by Giuseppe Tovini, a Catholic lawyer who wanted a bank for Catholic money, and Milan has called it the priests' bank ever since. Its principal shareholder is the Institute for the Works of Religion, the Vatican's own bank. Calvi joins it as a clerk in 1947, on Via Clerici, a short street behind the Piazza Cordusio. He is twenty-seven, and he will still be walking into this building thirty-five years later. He marries in 1952.
suggested_refs: Banco Ambrosiano, Via Clerici 2, Milan, founded 1896 by Giuseppe Tovini

stops.name: Via Clerici, personal assistant to Canesi
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1958 (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi: '1958: assistente personale di Alessandro Canesi'); month and day not given. An earlier pass of this research placed the appointment in 1947, which is only the year he joined the bank as a clerk; the correction is recorded in the report. The 1960 move to the foreign sector is from the same Italian article.
stops.campa: Eleven years at the counter, and then, in 1958, the promotion: he is made personal assistant to Alessandro Canesi, a leading figure of the bank and later its president. From that chair he sees how the Ambrosiano actually works, which is not how its balance sheet says it works. The lira is not freely convertible, and money that wants to leave Italy needs a route out; in this house the routes are drawn by whoever runs the foreign sector. In 1960 Calvi is put in charge of the bank's foreign financial operations.
suggested_refs: Alessandro Canesi, president of the Banco Ambrosiano, and the bank's foreign-sector desk after 1960

stops.name: Lugano, the Banca del Gottardo
stops.date_confidence: 1963 attested as the year the Swiss arm enters the group (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano); no month or day. Canonical atlas pin, inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json and paul_marcinkus.journey.json, both of which stage the same counter for the same structure.
stops.campa: Lugano is forty miles from Milan and in another country, which is the point of it. The Banca del Gottardo enters the Ambrosiano group in 1963 as its Swiss arm, and for the next twenty years the group's real business will pass through its accounts. Calvi does not build it. He inherits it, and then he learns what it is for. The same counter turns up in the papers of Licio Gelli and of Paul Marcinkus, the archbishop who runs the Vatican's bank, because whatever the three of them moved over two decades, a great deal of it moved through here.
suggested_refs: Banca del Gottardo, Lugano, Swiss subsidiary of the Banco Ambrosiano from 1963
sources: licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Lugano, the Banco del Gottardo'
paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'Lugano, the accounts at the Banca del Gottardo'

stops.name: Luxembourg City, the holding company
stops.date_confidence: decade marker only. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano places Banco Ambrosiano Holding in the 1970s expansion without a year, and it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano names Luxembourg among the group's low-tax jurisdictions with no date at all. An earlier pass gave 1963, which is the Banca del Gottardo date carried over in error. The stop sits between the 1963 Lugano stop and the 1971 promotion so that the segment runs forward; the marker is not a founding date. Coordinates are Luxembourg City.
stops.campa: Banco Ambrosiano Holding is registered in Luxembourg and it is not a bank in any sense a depositor would recognize. It is a place where ownership is kept. Beneath it sit companies in the Bahamas and, later, in Panama, and beneath those sit the loans the Milan balance sheet cannot show. Calvi assembles the structure across the decade, adding a layer whenever a layer is needed. The Bank of Italy's inspectors will spend years trying to see through it and will conclude, when they finally do, that there is nothing at the bottom of it.
suggested_refs: Banco Ambrosiano Holding, Luxembourg, apex of the group's offshore structure

stops.name: Via Clerici, direttore generale
stops.date_confidence: the year 1971 is attested on both the English and the Italian articles and corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano; the precise day, 16 February 1971, comes from it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi and was carried as a reconstruction, not an attestation, through the research pass.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of February 1971 Calvi is named direttore generale of the Banco Ambrosiano. He is fifty. He keeps the manner he arrived with in 1947, quiet and exact and badly at ease in company, and his subordinates find him no easier to read as a chief than as a clerk. The bank he now runs is small beside the Banca Commerciale Italiana he left, and pious, and it is about to become one of the busiest conduits of unaccountable money in Europe. Within the year it will have a Nassau subsidiary with an archbishop on the board.
suggested_refs: The general management of the Banco Ambrosiano under Calvi, from February 1971

stops.name: Nassau, the Cisalpine Overseas Bank
stops.date_confidence: 1971 attested for the founding, via michele_sindona.journey.json, stop 'Nassau, the Cisalpine Overseas Bank'; no month or day. Canonical atlas pin, inherited byte-identical from that file and from paul_marcinkus.journey.json. Marcinkus's own file dates his arrival on the Nassau board to 1972; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Marcinkus dates his IOR presidency from 1971 and records the Ambrosiano Overseas directorship without a year.
stops.campa: In Nassau, in 1971, three men put their names to a bank. Michele Sindona, the Sicilian financier whose pyramid is at its full height; Paul Marcinkus, the American archbishop just made head of the Institute for the Works of Religion; and Calvi. The Cisalpine Overseas Bank has the Bahamas for a jurisdiction and the Vatican for a shareholder, and neither the Bank of Italy nor anyone else in Rome can see inside it. It is registered offshore and capitalized from Milan, and the pope's bank holds shares in it from the first day.
suggested_refs: Cisalpine Overseas Bank, Nassau, founded 1971; later Banco Ambrosiano Overseas
sources: michele_sindona.journey.json, stop 'Nassau, the Cisalpine Overseas Bank'
paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'Nassau, a bishop on an offshore board'

stops.name: Vatican City, the Torrione di Niccolo V
stops.date_confidence: the year orders the segment rather than dating a meeting: Marcinkus heads the IOR from 1971 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Marcinkus) and his own atlas file dates the Nassau directorship to 1972. Canonical atlas pin, inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json, paul_marcinkus.journey.json and michele_sindona.journey.json; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_the_Works_of_Religion gives 41.90378, 12.45669 for the Torrione, about 275 m away.
stops.campa: The Institute for the Works of Religion occupies a squat medieval tower inside the Vatican walls, the Torrione raised by Nicholas V. Its head from 1971 is Paul Marcinkus, a Chicago priest who came up as Paul VI's bodyguard and interpreter and who now sits on the board of Calvi's Nassau bank. Two institutions are locked together: a Milanese commercial bank whose largest shareholder is the pope's bank, and the pope's bank, whose money is placed abroad by the Milanese banker. The Bank of Italy has no standing inside the Vatican walls, and the Vatican keeps no inspectors in Milan.
suggested_refs: The Torrione di Niccolo V, seat of the Institute for the Works of Religion
sources: Wikipedia (English), 'Institute for the Works of Religion'
paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'The Institute for the Works of Religion, made president'

stops.name: Via Clerici, the presidency
stops.date_confidence: 1975 attested on both language articles and on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano; the precise day, 15 October 1975, and the 1974 vice-presidency come from it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi and were carried as reconstruction. The 'banchiere di Dio' epithet is confirmed on both English articles but is not dated by any fetched source.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of October 1975, after a year as vice-president, Calvi becomes president of the Banco Ambrosiano. He is at the top of a bank of the second rank fitted with an offshore apparatus of the first, and the two halves of the institution have long since stopped describing the same business. The Italian press has already settled on the name it will use for him, for the Vatican shareholding and the archbishop on his offshore boards and the pious charter of 1896: il banchiere di Dio.
stops.quote_source: Press epithet for Calvi, Italian 'Banchiere di Dio', recorded in Wikipedia (English), 'Roberto Calvi' and 'Banco Ambrosiano'
suggested_refs: Rupert Cornwell, God's Banker: The Life and Death of Roberto Calvi (Victor Gollancz, 1983)

stops.name: Milan, the crash gets a name
stops.date_confidence: 1974 attested for the collapse (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michele_Sindona); April is the month michele_sindona.journey.json gives, and the pin is inherited byte-identical from that file. The widely printed claim that Sindona was Calvi's banking mentor could not be confirmed with a dated record on any encyclopedic page fetched in this pass; the 1971 Nassau venture above is the one jointly attested undertaking, and it is cited from the atlas rather than from the press.
stops.campa: Michele Sindona's pyramid comes down in 1974. The Franklin National Bank on Long Island, which he bought two years earlier, fails in the largest American bank collapse to that date, and Milan gives the wreck a name of its own: il crack Sindona. Since 1969 he has been moving large sums through the Vatican's bank and on into Swiss accounts, and the failure runs back along that route. The Vatican loses some thirty million dollars in the collapse. Calvi is not indicted, is not publicly named, and goes on running the Ambrosiano.
suggested_refs: Franklin National Bank, Mineola, Long Island, failed 8 October 1974
sources: michele_sindona.journey.json, stop 'Milan, the crash gets a name'

stops.name: Milan, the five point six million
stops.date_confidence: attested via michele_sindona.journey.json, stop 'Milan, the five point six million' (1977-01-01), whose pin is inherited byte-identical here; no month or day. The identification of the two unnamed recipients as Marcinkus and Calvi is the investigators' reading as recorded in that file, not a self-identification in the document.
stops.campa: Giorgio Ambrosoli, the lawyer appointed to liquidate Sindona's Italian banks, goes through the wreckage line by line and finds a commission of five point six million dollars paid out of the Sindona group to, as the paperwork has it, an American bishop and a Milanese banker. Investigators read the two descriptions as Marcinkus and Calvi. Ambrosoli writes it down. Nothing is charged against either man on the strength of it, and in July 1979 Ambrosoli is shot dead outside his own door in Milan by a gunman hired in New York.
suggested_refs: Giorgio Ambrosoli's liquidation papers on the Banca Privata Italiana
sources: michele_sindona.journey.json, stops 'Milan, the five point six million' and 'Milan, via Morozzo della Rocca'

stops.name: Via Clerici, the Bank of Italy predicts disaster
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano); no month given by any fetched source. Canonical Ambrosiano pin.
stops.campa: Inspectors of the Bank of Italy go into the Ambrosiano in 1978 and write a report using a word central bankers do not use: disaster, future and certain. The offshore holdings cannot be reconciled, the lending to companies nobody can identify is enormous, and the Milan books show none of it. The structure they are describing runs back to the Swiss arm of 1963 and no Italian authority has yet looked into it with the power to act on what it found. The report goes to the magistrates, and criminal investigations open.
suggested_refs: The 1978 Bank of Italy inspection report on the Banco Ambrosiano

stops.name: Milan, the inquiry loses its magistrate
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Alessandrini gives 29 January 1979, the ambush on his way to the Palazzo di Giustizia, and the Prima Linea commando of Sergio Segio, Marco Donat-Cattin and Michele Viscardi. An earlier pass dated the killing to 1978, the year of the Bank of Italy report itself; that is corrected here. General city coordinates: the street of the ambush is not given by the fetched source. No source connects the killing to the bank.
stops.campa: Emilio Alessandrini is the Milanese magistrate working the Ambrosiano file. On the morning of the twenty-ninth of January 1979 a commando of Prima Linea, a left-wing armed group, stops his car on his way to the Palazzo di Giustizia and shoots him dead. The Ambrosiano file loses the magistrate who was reading it. Sergio Segio, Marco Donat-Cattin and Michele Viscardi are acting out of their own politics and not out of anybody's banking interests, and nothing in the record ties the killing to the bank.
suggested_refs: Emilio Alessandrini, sostituto procuratore of Milan, killed by Prima Linea, 29 January 1979

stops.name: Via Solferino, the Corriere della Sera
stops.date_confidence: the Rizzoli purchase itself is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano, which places it loosely within the 1970s expansion) but is not dated to a month by any fetched source. The 'April 1981' date and the forty per cent figure circulate in secondary accounts and could not be confirmed in this pass; neither is asserted in the campa. Coordinates are the geocode for the Corriere building at Via Solferino 28; an earlier pass gave a pin about 200 m off.
stops.campa: Ambrosiano money buys into the Rizzoli group, which owns the Corriere della Sera, and Calvi's reach extends from the accounts of Italian business into its opinions. Via Solferino is the address of the most serious newspaper in the country. What is bought is not a printing press but a position: a bank whose real ownership is a secret takes a share in the institution whose work is to find such things out. The deal is structured out of the Milan office. Rizzoli will be sold on to Gemina in 1984, two years after Calvi is dead.
suggested_refs: The Corriere della Sera building, Via Solferino 28, Milan; the Rizzoli holding and its 1984 sale to Gemina

stops.name: Castiglion Fibocchi, the roll in the company archive
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda_2 gives the date, the magistrates Gherardo Colombo and Giuliano Turone, the searched premises and the discovery of the roll 'fra gli archivi della Giole', and the publication of the list by Arnaldo Forlani on 21 May 1981. Canonical atlas pin, inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json. An earlier pass had the list found at Villa Wanda and the search carried out by Milan police; both are corrected here.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of March 1981 the magistrates Gherardo Colombo and Giuliano Turone, working the Sindona fake-kidnapping case, have Licio Gelli's premises searched: Villa Wanda at Arezzo, the Socam works, and the Giole textile factory at Castiglion Fibocchi. In the Giole archive they find a list. Nine hundred and sixty-two names, generals and admirals and prefects and magistrates and journalists and bankers, all sworn into a masonic lodge that officially does not meet. Calvi's name is on it. Arnaldo Forlani reads the list into public record on the twenty-first of May.
suggested_refs: The Propaganda Due membership roll seized at the Giole factory, Castiglion Fibocchi, 17 March 1981
sources: licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Castiglion Fibocchi, the roll in the company archive'

stops.name: Milan, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested for Milan and 21 May 1981 on the order of the magistrate Gerardo D'Ambrosio (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi: 'arrestato a Milano per esportazione illecita di valuta'). en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives neither the city nor the day, and an earlier pass placed the arrest in Rome on 20 May; that is corrected here. General city coordinates: the site of the arrest is not recorded.
stops.campa: On the same day the P2 roll is read out in public, the twenty-first of May 1981, Calvi is arrested in Milan on the order of the magistrate Gerardo D'Ambrosio. The apparatus that made the offshore structure survivable is in the newspapers that morning, name by name, his own among them. He is sixty-one and has been president of the bank for six years. The charge is the illegal export of currency: twenty-seven million dollars taken out of Italy against the exchange controls.
suggested_refs: The currency-export proceeding of magistrate Gerardo D'Ambrosio, Milan, May 1981

stops.name: Milan, the barbiturates in the cell
stops.date_confidence: the attempt in custody is attested on both language articles; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives the method as barbiturates ('ingerendo barbiturici') and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives only the fact. Neither gives a month, so June orders the stop between the 21 May arrest and the sentencing. An earlier pass had him cutting his wrists and placed the attempt after his release on bail, which inverts the sequence; both are corrected here. No fetched source names the prison, and Lodi and San Vittore both circulate without confirmation.
stops.campa: In custody during his trial Calvi swallows barbiturates and is found in time. He offers no account of it afterward, and his family will put it down to the strain of the prosecution. It is the first sign in the record that the man Milan finds unreadable is under a pressure with nothing to do with the currency charge in front of the court. He is a banker in a cell whose real creditors are not in the courtroom and cannot be spoken about there. Which prison held him the sources do not say.
suggested_refs: The custodial phase of Calvi's 1981 currency trial

stops.name: Milan, four years suspended
stops.date_confidence: the four-year suspended sentence, the fine of roughly $19.8 million and the $27 million exported are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi) but no fetched source gives a day; July 1981 comes from the research pass. Coordinates are the geocode for the Palazzo di Giustizia, Via Carlo Freguglia 1; the atlas carries three slightly different pins for this building (45.4611/9.1968, 45.4622/9.2007, 45.4622/9.2019) and they are not reconciled here. The quotation is dated by its source only to the period after the May 1981 arrest and trial.
stops.campa: The court gives him four years, suspended, and a fine of about nineteen point eight million dollars for exporting twenty-seven million abroad. He is released pending appeal and the board of the Banco Ambrosiano keeps him on as president, a convicted man running a bank under sentence. Milan is a city where that is noticed. Asked in this period whose bank it actually is that he runs, he gives the answer that will be quoted back at him for the rest of his life and for a good deal longer than that.
stops.quote: Il Banco Ambrosiano non è mio, io sono soltanto il servitore di qualcuno
stops.quote_source: Roberto Calvi, after the May 1981 arrest and trial, quoted in Wikipedia (Italian), 'Roberto Calvi', section 'Crisi del Banco Ambrosiano'. Translation: 'Banco Ambrosiano is not mine, I am only somebody's servant.'
suggested_refs: Palazzo di Giustizia, Via Carlo Freguglia 1, Milan

stops.name: Vatican City, the letters of patronage
stops.date_confidence: the date comes from paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'The Institute for the Works of Religion, the letters of patronage' (1981-09-01), and the interlock pass notes that Marcinkus's file dates Calvi's counter-letter five days earlier. The letters themselves are real and repeatedly reported, but en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Marcinkus, the page cited for them in this research pass, documents only his IOR presidency and his Ambrosiano Overseas directorship; the letters therefore need a separate citation before they can carry an attested tag. Canonical IOR pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: The Panamanian companies holding the Ambrosiano's unrecoverable debt have to belong to somebody. In September 1981 the Institute for the Works of Religion signs letters acknowledging that they belong to it. Marcinkus signs. They are lettere di patronage, comfort letters, and they say the Vatican owns the shells; a separate letter from Calvi releases the Vatican from any liability arising out of them. Both documents exist, dated days apart, and each was written so that the other would never have to be produced.
suggested_refs: The IOR letters of patronage of September 1981 and Calvi's release letter
sources: paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'The Institute for the Works of Religion, the letters of patronage'
licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Vatican City, the Institute for Religious Works'

stops.name: Milan, the hole in the accounts
stops.date_confidence: the $1.287 billion figure is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano) and the 1 June date is inherited from licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Milan, the hole in the accounts', together with the canonical pin, byte-identical.
stops.campa: On the first of June 1982 the Bank of Italy puts a number on it. The Banco Ambrosiano cannot account for one billion two hundred and eighty-seven million dollars, advanced to Panamanian companies owned, on paper, by the Vatican. There is no asset behind the loans and there never was. The money went out to buy the bank's own shares and to fill the holes left by earlier lending, and some of it went to people whose names appear nowhere in the ledgers. For a few more days the announcement has not been made and Calvi is still, formally, the president of the bank.
suggested_refs: The Bank of Italy's June 1982 accounting of the Ambrosiano shortfall
sources: licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Milan, the hole in the accounts'

stops.name: Via Clerici, the letter to the pope
stops.date_confidence: the date and the quoted clause are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi), confirmed on two separate fetches; the article prints only this excerpt and not the full letter. The source gives the place only as Italy. The pin is Milan, where the Italian chronology puts him until his departure on 7 June; paul_marcinkus.journey.json stages the same date at the Vatican, which is the letter's destination and Marcinkus's own ground, not Calvi's.
stops.campa: The Institute for the Works of Religion is his largest shareholder and his largest problem, and on the fifth of June 1982 Calvi writes over Marcinkus's head, straight to John Paul II. He sets out what is coming for the Church if the Ambrosiano falls and the ownership of the Panamanian companies becomes public, and he asks for help that does not arrive. He has thirteen days to live. Whether the letter reached the pope's desk, and what was done with it if it did, the Vatican has never said.
stops.quote: provoke a catastrophe of unimaginable proportions in which the Church will suffer the gravest damage
stops.quote_source: Roberto Calvi, letter to Pope John Paul II, 5 June 1982, quoted in Wikipedia (English), 'Roberto Calvi'
suggested_refs: Calvi's letter of 5 June 1982 to John Paul II
sources: paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'The Institute for the Works of Religion, the bank goes down'

stops.name: Via Clerici, the fifth-floor window
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi puts both events on the day before the body was found, 17 June 1982: 'Calvi was stripped of his post at Banco Ambrosiano by the Bank of Italy, and his private secretary Graziella Corrocher jumped to her death from a fifth-floor window.' An earlier pass left the day open between 17 and 19 June; the uncertainty is removed. Canonical Ambrosiano pin.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of June the Bank of Italy strips Calvi of the presidency. He is not in Milan to be told of it; he is in a rented flat in Chelsea under another man's name. That day his private secretary, Graziella Corrocher, who has kept his diary and his appointments for years, leaves a note denouncing him. It is the first plain account of the bank's affairs written down by anyone inside it. Then she goes out of a fifth-floor window and dies in the courtyard below.
suggested_refs: Graziella Corrocher's note, Banco Ambrosiano, 17 June 1982

stops.name: Milan, the false passport
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives 7 June for the departure from Milan and the false passport in the name 'Gian Roberto Calvini'. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi instead has him disappear from his Rome apartment on 10 June and travel via Venice and Zurich; there is no Zurich leg in the Italian account and the two routes are not reconciled here. General city coordinates.
stops.campa: On the seventh of June, six days after the Bank of Italy puts its number on the hole and ten days before his own removal, Calvi leaves Milan. He carries a passport in the name of Gian Roberto Calvini, procured through Flavio Carboni, a Sardinian businessman whose trade is introductions. He is sixty-two years old, born in this city, employed in its banks since he was twenty-seven. He goes out of it under another man's name, with the bank still nominally his.
suggested_refs: The passport in the name Gian Roberto Calvini

stops.name: Rome, the guide assigned
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi puts him in Rome on 9 June, where Carboni assigns Emilio Pellicani as his guide. General city coordinates: the flat is not located by any fetched source, and the English article's separate claim that he vanished from a Rome apartment on 10 June is left standing beside this without adjudication.
stops.campa: He is in Rome on the ninth of June. Carboni assigns him a guide, Emilio Pellicani, and the flight takes the shape it will keep to the end: no schedule, no announced destination, each leg fixed a day in advance by men Calvi has no reason to trust and no alternative to. The Rome flat is the last address in Italy where the people around him know who he is. The English account has him disappearing from a Rome apartment on the tenth instead, with no guide in it at all, and the two chronologies are nowhere reconciled.
suggested_refs: Emilio Pellicani, assigned by Flavio Carboni as Calvi's guide, Rome, June 1982

stops.name: Venice, the flight north
stops.date_confidence: attested for 11 June (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi), which gives the flight to Venice and the onward journey by car to Trieste. Silvano Vittor's presence is attested from the same article and from the 2005 indictment; his description as a border smuggler is the common account and is not separately confirmed by the fetched sources.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of June he flies to Venice. The city is a hundred miles from the Yugoslav frontier and the frontier is what he wants. He is travelling with Silvano Vittor, hired out of the Trieste border country as a bodyguard, and by now the arrangement has inverted itself: the fugitive banker is entirely in the hands of the men moving him. From Venice they go on by car, east along the Adriatic road, toward the border country Vittor was hired out of.
suggested_refs: The Venice leg of the June 1982 flight

stops.name: Trieste, the last Italian city
stops.date_confidence: the Venice-to-Trieste car journey is attested (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi) but not dated; 12 June orders the stop between the attested 11 June and 14 June. The motorboat crossing into Yugoslav waters is carried in the same article and was tagged as reconstruction in this research pass; no fetched source gives the crossing point, and the approximate Istrian coordinate an earlier pass used has been folded into this Trieste stop rather than pinned separately.
stops.campa: Trieste is the end of Italy, a port shoved up against a border, and Vittor's own country. Here the party leaves the roads for the water: a motorboat out into Yugoslav waters and back onto land beyond the checkpoints, the oldest trick on this coast and the reason smugglers live here at all. Calvi crosses out of the state whose central bank has just published the size of his hole and whose courts hold his conviction. From the far shore the route turns inland and north, into Austria.
suggested_refs: The Trieste border country and the sea crossing of June 1982

stops.name: Bregenz, at the Austrian border
stops.date_confidence: attested for 14 June and for Carboni meeting him at Bregenz (it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi). The overland leg through Klagenfurt in Carinthia is carried in the same chronology and was tagged as reconstruction in this pass; it is described here rather than given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of June Carboni meets him at Bregenz, on the Austrian shore of Lake Constance, Switzerland on one side and Germany on the other and a private aviation field inside an hour. The road has come up through Carinthia to get here. Calvi has been moving for a week and has slept in a different country most nights. The men around him are Carboni, who arranged the passport, and Vittor, who knows the borders; nobody from the bank is with him and no lawyer has been sent for.
suggested_refs: Bregenz, Vorarlberg, meeting point of 14 June 1982

stops.name: Innsbruck, the private jet
stops.date_confidence: attested; it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives the Innsbruck-London private flight on 15 June. The London airfield is not named by any fetched source.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of June a chartered jet lifts off from Innsbruck for London. It is the last leg and the only one that leaves a clean record, because private aviation files flight plans. Calvi has chosen England and the choice has a logic: London is where the Ambrosiano's Eurodollar business was done, where creditors might conceivably be talked to, and where no Italian warrant runs. He is travelling as Gian Roberto Calvini and has been for eight days. He lands with three of them left.
suggested_refs: The Innsbruck-London charter flight of 15 June 1982

stops.name: Chelsea Cloisters, the last address
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi confirms the lodging at 'Chelsea Cloister' with Silvano Vittor and the arrival of Carboni and the Kleinszig sisters from Amsterdam on 16 June. He flew in on 15 June, so the stay runs from 15 or 16 June to the night of the 17th; an earlier pass gave '16-18 June', which overstates the far end, since the body was found at 7:30 on the morning of the 18th. Coordinates are the geocode for Chelsea Cloisters, Sloane Avenue SW3 3DD, about 250 m from the pin used in the earlier pass.
stops.campa: Chelsea Cloisters on Sloane Avenue is a large block of serviced flats, the kind of building where nobody asks. Calvi takes a room there with Vittor. On the sixteenth Carboni arrives from Amsterdam with Manuela and Michaela Kleinszig. Calvi makes telephone calls and the content of them is not known. He is a man of exact habits sitting in a rented room on a false passport, waiting for something to be arranged on his behalf by people who have not told him what it is. On the night of the seventeenth he goes out.
suggested_refs: Chelsea Cloisters, Sloane Avenue, London SW3, Calvi's last lodging

stops.name: London, Blackfriars Bridge
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banco_Ambrosiano both give the morning of 18 June 1982, the scaffolding, the bricks and the roughly $14,000 in three currencies. Canonical atlas pin, inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackfriars_Bridge gives 51 30 35 N, 0 06 16 W, that is 51.5097, -0.1044, about 130 m away. The 'frati neri' self-description of the P2 lodge is confirmed by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi, which asserts no causal link between it and the bridge.
stops.campa: At half past seven on the morning of the eighteenth of June 1982 a body is seen hanging from the scaffolding under Blackfriars Bridge. It is Calvi. There are bricks and stones in his pockets and about fourteen thousand dollars in three currencies, and his watch is still on his wrist. The tide is out. The members of Licio Gelli's lodge called themselves the frati neri, the black friars, and the bridge takes its name from the Dominican priory that stood on the north bank; whether the two facts have anything to do with each other, nothing in the record establishes.
stops.quote: Calvi è stato assassinato, e quelli che lo hanno ucciso hanno fatto apparire la cosa come una sorta di rituale massonico
stops.quote_source: Michele Sindona, interview with Nick Tosches before his own death in prison in 1986, cited in Wikipedia (Italian), 'Roberto Calvi'. Translation: 'Calvi was murdered, and those who killed him made it look like a kind of masonic ritual.' The original Tosches interview text could not be reached in this pass.
suggested_refs: Blackfriars Bridge, London, and the site of the Dominican priory on its north bank
Philip Willan, The Last Supper: The Mafia, the Masons and the Killing of Roberto Calvi (2007)

stops.name: The City of London, the first inquest
stops.date_confidence: the suicide verdict of the first inquest is attested for July 1982 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi); no day is given. Sir Keith Simpson's testimony that there were no signs of struggle comes from the research crawl and was tagged as reconstruction, not confirmed against a fetched source. The courtroom is not located by any fetched source; the coordinates approximate the City of London Guildhall area.
stops.campa: A coroner's jury sits in the City of London in July 1982 and returns, by majority, a verdict of suicide. The pathologist Sir Keith Simpson tells the court there are no marks of a struggle on the body. Nothing at the inquest explains how a man of sixty-two with no history of climbing got himself down onto scaffolding under a bridge at low tide with his pockets full of masonry, and nothing has to: a suicide verdict requires the death to be self-inflicted, not the method to be plausible. The family refuses the verdict from the day it is handed down.
suggested_refs: The first City of London inquest into Calvi's death, July 1982

stops.name: Drezzo, the grave in Como province
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives Drezzo as the original burial place without a date; August 1982 orders the stop after the July inquest and is not an attested date. Drezzo is a frazione of Colverde since the 2014 merger with Pare and Gironico; coordinates from it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drezzo (45 49 N, 9 00 E). An earlier pass gave a pin about 5 km northwest.
stops.campa: With the London verdict of suicide standing, Calvi is buried at Drezzo, a village in the province of Como near the Swiss border, in the hills above the lake and forty miles from the office on Via Clerici. A suicide verdict has consequences past the reputation of the dead: it voids the life insurance and it complicates the burial. The family takes him back to the province, sixteen years before anyone will disturb the grave again. The stone gives his name and his dates and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The cemetery at Drezzo, Colverde, province of Como

stops.name: The City of London, the open verdict
stops.date_confidence: attested for July 1983 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi); no day given. The quashing of the first verdict on appeal is the standard account of how the second inquest came to be convened and is not separately confirmed by the fetched sources. Courtroom location approximate, as above.
stops.campa: A second inquest is convened in July 1983 and this jury declines to say what happened. An open verdict means the court has heard the evidence and cannot determine whether the man killed himself or was killed by somebody else. In English law it is the honest answer, and it is also the end of the matter: without a finding of unlawful killing there is nothing for a police force to open a file on. Did anyone go down onto the scaffolding with him? The jury heard what evidence there was and would not say.
suggested_refs: The second City of London inquest and its open verdict, July 1983

stops.name: Geneva, the Vatican pays the creditors
stops.date_confidence: the date and the Geneva venue are inherited from paul_marcinkus.journey.json, stop 'Geneva, the Vatican pays the creditors' (1984-05-25), whose pin is used byte-identical. The sum is contested: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives US$224 million to 120 creditors in 1984, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Marcinkus gives GBP 145 million with no year, and the atlas file and the research crawl both carry $250 million. The $224 million figure is used here and the disagreement is left open.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of May 1984 the Institute for the Works of Religion signs a settlement in Geneva with the creditors of the collapsed Banco Ambrosiano. The record gives the sum as two hundred and twenty-four million dollars, paid to a hundred and twenty creditors in recognition of moral involvement, with no admission of legal liability and no acknowledgement that the Panamanian companies were ever the Vatican's. Marcinkus is never charged with anything. Other accounts of the same settlement put the payment at a hundred and forty-five million pounds, or at two hundred and fifty million dollars, and the figure has never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: The 1984 IOR settlement with the Ambrosiano creditors

stops.name: London, the shoes without rust
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives the family's engagement of Kroll Associates in 1991, the assignment of Jeff Katz, and the October 1992 delivery of the report to the UK home secretary and the City of London Police. No day is given. The stop is pinned at the bridge, whose scaffolding the report concerns; no source gives an address for the examination itself.
stops.campa: In 1991 Calvi's family hires Kroll Associates and the investigator Jeff Katz goes back to the scaffolding. His forensic report turns on the shoes: they carry neither the rust nor the paint that scaffolding leaves on anything that touches it. A man who did not walk on the scaffolding did not hang himself from it. Katz delivers the report in October 1992 to the home secretary and to the City of London Police, ten years after the death and nine after the open verdict closed the English proceedings. It is received and filed.
suggested_refs: The Kroll Associates forensic report on Calvi's shoes, October 1992

stops.name: Milan, the coffin opened
stops.date_confidence: December 1998 is attested for the exhumation on the order of an Italian court (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi); it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi names the investigating judge Otello Lupacchini as the source of the order but does not give the day. The Milan forensic institute and these general city coordinates were tagged as reconstruction in the research pass: no fetched source gives the laboratory's address.
stops.campa: In December 1998 an Italian judge orders the body exhumed. Calvi comes out of the ground at Drezzo and goes to a forensic institute for the examination the London inquests never made: the neck, the vertebrae, the marks that separate a man who drops with a rope around his neck from a man lifted with one already there. Sixteen years of decay have taken most of the evidence. What is left will be enough. The order comes from the investigating judge Otello Lupacchini, after years of pressure from the family.
suggested_refs: The December 1998 exhumation and second autopsy

stops.name: Tremenico, the family chapel
stops.date_confidence: it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi records the reinterment in the family edicola at Tremenico without a date; 1999 orders the stop after the December 1998 exhumation and is not attested. Coordinates from it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremenico (46 04 33.24 N, 9 21 58.32 E). An earlier pass placed Tremenico in the Valsassina, which is the wrong valley, and about 4.5 km off the mark.
stops.campa: After the second autopsy the family does not take him back to Drezzo. He goes instead into the family chapel at Tremenico, a village of a few hundred people at seven hundred and fifty metres in the Valvarrone, above the eastern arm of Lake Como. It is a hard place to reach and a harder one to find. The comune of Valvarrone does not exist yet; it will be assembled in 2018 out of Introzzo, Tremenico and Vestreno, and the village will stop being a comune and become a name inside one.
suggested_refs: The Calvi family edicola in the cemetery at Tremenico, Valvarrone, province of Lecco

stops.name: The City of London, the murder inquiry
stops.date_confidence: both events attested by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi: the German forensic report published October 2002, finding the neck injuries inconsistent with self-inflicted hanging, and the City of London Police reopening the case as a murder inquiry in September 2003. Neither carries a day, and the German scientist is not named by the source. The two are combined in one stop; the coordinates approximate the City of London.
stops.campa: A German forensic scientist commissioned by the Italian court publishes in October 2002: the injuries to Calvi's neck are not those of a self-inflicted hanging. In September 2003 the City of London Police reopen the file as a murder investigation, twenty-one years after two coroner's juries failed to get there. The suicide of 1982 is formally dead. What replaces it is an inquiry and not an answer. The scene under the bridge was cleared in a morning twenty-one years earlier, and the bank whose papers would matter has not existed since.
suggested_refs: The October 2002 German forensic report; the City of London Police murder inquiry of September 2003

stops.name: Rome, Piazzale Clodio, the Calvi file
stops.date_confidence: 19 July 2005 is attested for Gelli's indictment (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licio_Gelli) and the pin is inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json, stop 'Rome, Piazzale Clodio, the Calvi file'. Gelli's courtroom statement is given by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi only in reported speech, never inside quotation marks, so it is paraphrased here and not quoted. The dropping of the case in May 2009 is attested on the same two articles.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of July 2005 Licio Gelli is indicted in Rome in connection with the murder. He is eighty-six and has already been convicted in Milan over the Ambrosiano collapse. In court he denies involvement, says Calvi was murdered, and states that the killing was commissioned in the People's Republic of Poland; the newspapers print it and nobody carries it anywhere. His name is taken off the indictment before the trial proper begins, and in May 2009 the prosecutors drop the case against him for want of evidence that he planned or executed anything.
suggested_refs: The Rome prosecutors' Calvi file at Piazzale Clodio

stops.name: Rebibbia, the bunker courtroom
stops.date_confidence: 5 October 2005 and the five defendants are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi). The fortified 'aula bunker' at Rebibbia comes from the research crawl and is not confirmed by it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcere_di_Rebibbia, which does not mention one. Coordinates from that article for the Rebibbia complex at Ponte Mammolo (41 56 05.98 N, 12 34 28.51 E); an earlier pass was about 1 km off. The Carboni quotation is truncated by an ellipsis in its source.
stops.campa: The trial opens on the fifth of October 2005 in a fortified courtroom inside Rebibbia prison in Rome, the sort of room Italy builds when the defendants' associates are still at liberty. Five men stand accused: Giuseppe Calo, a Cosa Nostra boss known as the cashier; Flavio Carboni, who arranged the passport and the route; Manuela Kleinszig; Ernesto Diotallevi; and Silvano Vittor, who shared the flat at Chelsea Cloisters. The prosecution's case is that the money in the bank was other people's and that Calvi lost it.
stops.quote: Non capisco che interesse potevo avere a fare del male a Calvi
stops.quote_source: Flavio Carboni, trial testimony, quoted in Wikipedia (Italian), 'Roberto Calvi'. Translation: 'I don't understand what interest I could have had in harming Calvi.'
suggested_refs: The Rebibbia courtroom, Rome, and the 2005-2007 Calvi murder trial

stops.name: Rebibbia, all five acquitted
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi gives the date, the presiding judge Mario Lucio d'Andria, the insufficiency of evidence, and the court's finding that the death was murder rather than suicide. Same pin as the trial opening.
stops.campa: On the sixth of June 2007 Judge Mario Lucio d'Andria acquits all five for insufficient evidence, and in the same judgment the court holds that Roberto Calvi was murdered. Calo, Carboni, Kleinszig, Diotallevi and Vittor walk out of the Rebibbia courtroom. Both halves stand and neither cancels the other: an Italian court has established that the death was a killing and cannot say by whom. The London jury of 1983 declined to establish either. Twenty-five years have passed since the body came off the scaffolding.
suggested_refs: The judgment of 6 June 2007 in the Calvi murder trial

stops.name: Rome, Piazzale Clodio, the second death
stops.date_confidence: 7 May 2010 for the appeal confirming the acquittals of Calo, Carboni and Diotallevi, and 18 November 2011 for the Court of Cassation, are both attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Calvi). Tescaroli's remark is quoted verbatim in that article. The Piazzale Clodio venue for the appeal is an assumption from the research pass, not confirmed by any fetched source; the pin is the canonical one from licio_gelli.journey.json, used byte-identical. The Cassation ruling of 2011 is folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: An appeals court confirms the acquittals of Calo, Carboni and Diotallevi on the seventh of May 2010, and the Court of Cassation confirms them again on the eighteenth of November 2011, which ends the criminal case for good. The prosecutor Luca Tescaroli says Calvi has been murdered a second time. The appeal court's own written reasoning holds to the finding of 2007 and states it flatly. Nobody has ever been convicted of anything to do with the death of the president of the Banco Ambrosiano.
stops.quote: Roberto Calvi è stato ammazzato, non si è ucciso
stops.quote_source: Reasoning (motivazioni) of the Rome appeals court, ruling of 7 May 2010, quoted in Wikipedia (Italian), 'Roberto Calvi'. Translation: 'Roberto Calvi was killed, he did not kill himself.'
